findings.title: deleteMany with retryCount > 1 deletes ALL workflow reminders (including EMAIL and WHATSAPP), not just SMS
findings.body: The cleanup query at the top of the handler uses `OR: [{ method: SMS, scheduledDate <= now }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]`. The second OR branch has no `method` filter, so every WorkflowReminder row in the database with retryCount > 1 is deleted — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders that may be legitimately scheduled and pending. This causes silent loss of email/WhatsApp reminders for all users. The retryCount branch must be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and arguably also `scheduled: false`), e.g. `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

findings.title: Reminders with no message or no sendTo are silently skipped and never retried or cleaned up
findings.body: The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` (the else branch) or in the catch block. If `message` is empty/null (e.g. workflowStep has neither reminderBody nor template REMINDER) or `sendTo` is missing (e.g. SMS_NUMBER action with no sendTo configured, or booking without smsReminderNumber), the code falls through without scheduling, without incrementing retryCount, and without any error. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` forever and is re-fetched and re-processed by the cron on every run indefinitely — an infinite no-op loop and unbounded DB growth. These cases should either increment retryCount (so the cleanup deletes them) or be logged/handled explicitly.

findings.title: Read-modify-write of retryCount is not atomic; concurrent cron runs can lose increments
findings.body: The handler reads `retryCount` in the findMany (line 58) and later writes `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` (lines 184 and 195) based on that stale read. If the cron job runs concurrently (overlapping invocations, or the same reminder processed twice), both runs read the same value and write the same incremented value, so failures are undercounted and a reminder that failed twice may never reach retryCount > 1, defeating the retry limit. Use an atomic increment (`retryCount: { increment: 1 }`) instead of computing from the fetched value.

findings.title: Cleanup deletes SMS reminders whose scheduledDate has passed even if they were successfully scheduled and are still pending delivery
findings.body: The first OR branch deletes all SMS reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` regardless of the `scheduled` flag. A reminder that was successfully scheduled with Twilio (scheduled: true, referenceId set) but whose scheduledDate has just passed is deleted from the DB before we can confirm delivery/cancellation status. This was pre-existing behavior, but combined with the new retry logic it also means a successfully scheduled reminder is removed at its fire time, so any downstream logic that relies on the WorkflowReminder row (e.g. cancellation when a booking is cancelled/rescheduled) loses the referenceId needed to cancel the Twilio message. The delete should be scoped to `scheduled: false` (or the deletion of past-due rows should only apply to unscheduled/failed reminders).

findings.title: Unscheduled reminders query does not exclude reminders that already exhausted retries
findings.body: The findMany fetches all unscheduled SMS reminders within 7 days without filtering on retryCount. Reminders with retryCount >= 2 are only removed by the deleteMany at the start of the same run; between runs (or if the deleteMany fails/partially fails), they are re-fetched and re-processed, incrementing retryCount further and generating repeated Twilio attempts/log noise. Adding `retryCount: { lte: 1 }` to the where clause makes the retry cap robust and avoids wasted work.

findings.title: Failed retryCount update in catch block is not awaited error-handled; a DB failure here throws out of the loop iteration silently
findings.body: Inside the catch block, the `prisma.workflowReminder.update` call can itself throw (e.g. transient DB error). If it does, the exception propagates out of the for-loop and aborts processing of all remaining reminders in this run, and the outer handler never sends its 200 response (the request hangs until timeout). The update should be wrapped or the loop should be resilient so one bad row doesn't abort the whole batch.
